linkedin.title: We decided to build our news feed without a feedback loop that prioritizes outrage.
linkedin.body:
Most news algorithms are trained to maximize time spent on the app. The easiest way to keep someone scrolling is to show them content that makes them angry or anxious. It is a proven engagement strategy, but it is also a miserable way to consume information.

At Headlinne, we made a deliberate engineering choice to optimize for something else. Instead of chasing high-arousal emotions, we built our models to prioritize relevance and diversity of perspective. We want to show you the stories that actually matter to your specific interests, rather than the stories that are most likely to make you want to fight with a stranger in the comments.

This makes the development process harder. It is much simpler to build a machine that feeds on outrage than one that respects the user's attention. But we believe that if you provide people with a cleaner, more thoughtful signal, they will value the product more in the long run. We are betting that you want to be informed, not just agitated.
linkedin.cta: You can see how this approach feels at HEADLINNE.com.

instagram.title: NASA finds a rare new crater on the moon

slides.headline: NASA finds a rare new crater on the moon
slides.subtitle: The impact crater spans 728 feet across

slides.explanation: This crater is about the length of two American football fields laid end to end. It is a massive scar on the lunar surface caused by a single impact.

slides.headline: An event that happens only once a century
slides.explanation: While the moon is constantly hit by small space rocks, an impact of this specific size is extremely rare. Scientists estimate an event of this magnitude occurs only once every hundred years.
Both Engadget and Science Daily have verified the findings from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. You can trust this report.

slides.subtitle: Read the full story on Headlinne.

instagram.caption:
NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has captured images of a fresh impact crater on the moon.

It measures 728 feet wide.

Most lunar impacts involve tiny debris, but this one was significant. Experts say an impact of this size only happens about once a century.

It is a rare look at the violent history of our solar system happening in real time.

reels.title: Scientists discover cells that cheat death and rebuild damaged tissue
reels.hook: Scientists discover cells that cheat death and rebuild damaged tissue

beats.caption: Scientists discover cells that cheat death and rebuild damaged tissue
Imagine a house that repairs itself after a fire.
beats.narration: Imagine a house that could somehow repair itself after a fire. It sounds like sci-fi, but biology is doing it.

beats.caption: Scientists found cells that cheat death.
beats.narration: Scientists have found a specific population of cells that can actually survive their own programmed death process.

beats.caption: They survive destruction then rebuild tissue fast.
beats.narration: They don't just survive. They jumpstart the healing process to rapidly fix damaged tissue nearby.

beats.caption: Their descendants become tougher to damage.
beats.narration: And the descendants of these cells become far more resistant to future damage. They get stronger.

beats.caption: This same strength might help cancer return.
beats.narration: But there is a catch. The same mechanism that heals wounds could also help cancer cells return after treatment.

data.left_text: Could lead to better healing for injuries.
data.right_text: Might help cancer cells survive treatment.

beats.caption: Researchers are still figuring it out.
beats.narration: Researchers are still working to understand how to use this without the risks. It is early days.

beats.caption: Get the full story at Headlinne.com.
beats.narration: For more science news that matters, check out Headlinne.com. Would you want your cells to work this way?

story_card.headline: 37 Die in Nigerian Prison Cell
story_card.standfirst: Protests erupt in Minna following the deaths of detained goldminers.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text: Thirty-seven suspected illegal goldminers died in a prison cell run by a paramilitary group.

steps.label: How we got here
steps.text: Survivors described panic and suffocation while in custody earlier this week.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.text: The victims included many children. The incident has now sparked violent public protests.

steps.label: What to watch
steps.text: Police are firing teargas in Minna as tensions rise over the handling of these detainees.

story_card.caption:
Protests have broken out in Minna following the deaths of 37 suspected goldminers in a Nigerian prison cell.

Survivors of the incident describe a desperate struggle to breathe while being held by a paramilitary group. The situation is escalating as local police use teargas to manage crowds angered by the tragedy.

How should local authorities be held accountable when detainees die in custody?
